summary: Gives an overview of the protocol suite for real-time communication in browsers (WebRTC), meant as a starting point to find all required parts.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8825 is the map of the WebRTC protocol suite. It lists the parts a browser needs in order to place a live audio or video call, groups them by what they do, and points at the separate document that specifies each one. It also sets out the terms the rest of the suite uses, so that the individual documents agree with each other.

questions: what is the difference between the media path and the signalling path
subtitle: A roadmap listing which specifications a browser or device must implement for real-time audio, video and data.

tldr.problem: Real-time communication between browsers needs a set of protocols, and no single document could describe all of them without becoming unusable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8825 divides the WebRTC protocols into six functionality groups, from data transport up to presentation and control, and names the document that defines each one, marking which of them every implementation must support.
tldr.outcome: An implementer can read the roadmap and its references and have everything needed to build a WebRTC-compatible implementation, while the individual specifications stay narrow enough to be useful on their own.

today: RFC 8825 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is the roadmap to the WebRTC specifications: it names the documents that every implementation must follow, from the transports in RFC 8835 to the data channel establishment protocol in RFC 8832.

sections.title: Why a Roadmap
sections.content:
The Internet was considered early on as a vehicle for real-time interactive applications, most obviously audio conversations and video conferencing. The first attempts at such applications depended on special networks, special hardware and custom-built software, often at very high prices or of low quality, which put heavy demands on the infrastructure. As bandwidth increased and processors became faster, the barriers to participation fell, and a satisfactory experience became possible on ordinary computing hardware.

Barriers to universal communication remain. There is still no single set of communication protocols that everyone agrees should be made available, and there is a sheer lack of universal identification systems, of the kind served by telephone numbers or email addresses elsewhere. Development of a universal solution has proved hard.

A new platform has risen for deploying services: the browser-embedded application. As long as the browser platform has the necessary interfaces, almost any kind of service can be delivered on it. These interfaces were traditionally delivered by plugins that had to be downloaded and installed separately; with HTML5, application developers see promise in those interfaces becoming available in a standardized way inside the browser.

The memo describes a set of building blocks that can be made accessible and controllable through a JavaScript API in a browser, and that together form a sufficient set of functions for interactive audio and video in applications that communicate directly between browsers across the Internet. The resulting protocol suite is intended to enable all the applications described as required scenarios in the WebRTC use cases document. Other efforts, in the W3C working groups, focus on the standardized APIs; this memo concentrates on the protocols needed for the interactions over the network.

Operators are told to note that deploying WebRTC changes the nature of signalling for real-time media and may shift the kinds of devices used to create and consume it. Session setup will typically happen over TLS-secured web technologies using application-specific protocols, which means operational techniques that insert network elements to interpret the Session Description Protocol will not work with such signalling. The increase in browser-based communications may also lead to a shift away from dedicated real-time hardware such as SIP desk phones, which diminishes the efficacy of techniques that place such devices on their own segment, address range or VLAN for traffic filtering and quality of service.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time calls have always been possible, but for a long time they needed their own networks and their own devices. Once browsers could do it, the problem became a standards problem rather than an infrastructure problem. This RFC does not define a protocol; it says which protocols there are and which ones everybody has to implement.

sections.title: The Terms the Suite Defines
sections.content:
The total WebRTC effort has two major parts, each made of several documents: a protocol specification done in the IETF, and a JavaScript API specification defined in a series of W3C documents. Together they aim to provide an environment where JavaScript embedded in a page, when authorized by its user, can set up communication using audio, video and auxiliary data, as long as the browser supports the specifications.

The protocol specification does not assume that every implementation implements the API, and it is not necessary for interoperation to know whether the other party is a browser or another device implementing the protocol specification.

The document defines the terms used across the suite. An SDP Agent is the protocol implementation involved in the Session Description Protocol offer and answer exchange. An ICE Agent is an implementation of the Interactive Connectivity Establishment protocol, and may also be an SDP Agent. Signalling is the communication that establishes, manages and controls media paths and data paths, and the signalling path is the channels used to carry it, which may involve more entities than the media path does. A data channel is an abstraction that allows data to be sent between endpoints in the form of messages, and two endpoints can have several between them. The media path is the path that media data follows between two endpoints.

A WebRTC browser, also called a WebRTC user agent, conforms to both the protocol specification and the JavaScript API. A WebRTC non-browser conforms to the protocol specification but does not claim to implement the JavaScript API, and can also be called a WebRTC device or native application. A WebRTC endpoint is either of those. A WebRTC-compatible endpoint is one that can communicate with a WebRTC endpoint but may fail to meet some requirements, which may limit where in the network it can be attached or the security guarantees it offers. A WebRTC gateway is a WebRTC-compatible endpoint that mediates media traffic to non-WebRTC entities. Every WebRTC browser is a WebRTC endpoint, so any requirement on an endpoint applies to a browser as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite distinguishes a browser, which also offers a programming interface, from a device or server that speaks the same protocols but has no such interface. It also separates the signalling path, which runs through servers and sets the call up, from the media path, which is the direct connection the audio and video take.

sections.title: The Browser Model and the Functionality Groups
sections.content:
For browser-based applications the model does not assume the browser contains every function needed for something like a telephone or a video conference. The vision is that the browser has the functions a web application needs, working with its backend servers. Two vital interfaces therefore need specification: the protocols browsers use to talk to each other without intervening servers, and the APIs offered to a JavaScript application so it can use the browser's functions.

The diagram in the RFC shows the browser model: servers on one side, connected by the on-the-wire protocols; JavaScript, HTML and CSS in the page; and the browser's real-time function, which talks to the other browsers using the on-the-wire protocols and to the operating system underneath. There is no restriction that the protocols can only be used to talk to another browser, so any endpoint that implements them faithfully should interoperate with the application running in the browser.

The common deployment model is a trapezoid. The media path, the low path, goes directly between the browsers and has to conform to the WebRTC protocol suite, while the signalling path, the high path, goes via servers that can modify, translate or manipulate the signals as needed. If the two web servers are run by different entities, the mechanism between them has to be agreed, by standardization or otherwise, and existing protocols such as SIP or XMPP could be used.

The functionality groups are specified from the bottom up. Data transport covers TCP and UDP, the means of securely setting up connections, and the functions for deciding when to send data, such as congestion management and bandwidth estimation. Data framing covers RTP, SCTP, DTLS and other container formats, with their functions for confidentiality and integrity. Data formats covers codec specifications and formats for the data passed between systems. Connection management covers setting up connections, agreeing on data formats and changing them during a call. Presentation and control covers floor control, screen layout and voice-activated image switching, where part of the system needs cooperation between parties. Local system support functions are the functions each participant may implement as it chooses, without affecting what goes on the wire, such as echo cancellation, local authentication, operating system access control and local recording.

The first three groups form a media transport infrastructure and the last three form a media service. In many contexts it makes sense to use a common specification for the transport infrastructure, which can be embedded in browsers and accessed through standard interfaces, and let the service layer vary, although at least the first five groups need to be specified for interoperable services.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite is arranged in layers: get the data across the network, put it in a secure container, agree on a format, set the connection up, then handle the parts of a call that need both sides to cooperate. The first three layers are worth standardising together because they are the plumbing; the top three can vary between applications.

sections.title: Data Transport
sections.content:
Data transport refers to sending and receiving data over the network interfaces, the choice of network-layer addresses at each end of the communication, and the interaction with intermediate entities that handle the data but do not modify it, such as TURN relays. It includes the necessary functions for congestion control, retransmission and in-order delivery.

WebRTC endpoints must implement the transport protocols described in RFC 8835.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the bottom layer: UDP and TCP, the addresses used, and the machinery that decides how fast to send so the network does not collapse. A separate document, RFC 8835, says exactly which transports are used.

sections.title: Data Framing and Securing
sections.content:
The format for media transport is RTP. Implementation of the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol is required for all implementations. The detailed considerations for using functions from RTP and SRTP are in RFC 8834, the security considerations for the WebRTC use case are in RFC 8826, and the resulting security functions are described in RFC 8827.

Considerations for the transfer of data that is not in RTP format are described in RFC 8831, and a supporting protocol for establishing individual data channels is described in RFC 8832. WebRTC endpoints must implement these two specifications, and must also implement RFC 8834, RFC 8826, RFC 8827 and the requirements they include.
sections.plainLanguage: Media travels in RTP packets, and they must be protected with SRTP. Data channels, which carry ordinary application data rather than media, use a different container, SCTP, protected with DTLS. This section names the documents that define all of that.

sections.title: Data Formats
sections.content:
The intent of the specification is to allow each communications event to use the data formats best suited to that instance, where a format is supported by both sides of the connection. A minimum standard is greatly helpful so that communication can be achieved, so this document specifies a minimum baseline that will be supported by all implementations and leaves further codecs to the implementer's discretion.

WebRTC endpoints that support audio or video must implement the codecs and profiles required in RFC 7874 and RFC 7742.
sections.plainLanguage: Two peers have to agree on a codec, and a call fails if they cannot. The suite therefore fixes a small set of codecs that every implementation must have, and leaves everything else to the implementer.

sections.title: Connection Management
sections.content:
Setting up, negotiating and tearing down connections is a large subject, where both interoperability and freedom to innovate are desirable. Three principles apply.

First, the WebRTC media negotiations will be capable of representing the same SDP offer and answer semantics used in SIP, in such a way that a signalling gateway between SIP and the WebRTC media negotiation can be built. Second, it will be possible to gateway between legacy SIP devices that support ICE and the appropriate RTP and SDP mechanisms, codecs and security mechanisms without using a media gateway, though a signalling gateway may be needed to convert between signalling on the web side and SIP signalling. Third, when an SDP for a new codec is specified, no other standardization should be required for it to be possible to use that codec in web browsers: adding new codecs that might have new SDP parameters should not change the APIs between the browser and the JavaScript application, so that old applications written before the codec was specified can use it automatically where appropriate, with no changes to the JavaScript.

The particular choices made for WebRTC, and their implications for the API offered by a browser, are described in RFC 8829. WebRTC browsers must implement RFC 8829. WebRTC endpoints must implement the functions described there that relate to the network layer, such as BUNDLE, rtcp-mux and Trickle ICE, but do not need to support the API functionality it describes.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a call means exchanging descriptions of what each side can do and agreeing on it. The rules keep that exchange compatible with the older telephony world, so a gateway can be built, and they keep new codecs from forcing changes on applications that were written years earlier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security of web-enabled real-time communication comes in several pieces. The first is security of the components, the browsers and the other servers involved; the browser is probably the richest target, and the aim should be that the introduction of these components introduces no additional vulnerability.

The second is security of the communication channels. It should be easy for participants to reassure themselves of the security of their communication, by verifying the cryptographic parameters of the links they take part in and getting assurances from the other parties that appropriate measures are taken. The third is security of the partners' identities, verifying that the participants are who they say they are when positive identification is appropriate, or that their identities cannot be uncovered when anonymity is a goal of the application.

The security analysis and the requirements derived from it are in RFC 8826, and the security sections of the W3C media capture and WebRTC documents are also important.
sections.plainLanguage: The security argument has three parts: the software on each side should not add holes, the links themselves should be verifiable, and the identity of the other party should be either checked or hidden, depending on what the application wants. The detail sits in a separate document.
